profiles.why: PostHog's own pricing page describes a usage-based, pay-per-use model spread across many bundled products rather than one flat subscription (e.g. free up to 1 million events/mo then $0.00005/event for Product Analytics, $0.005/recording for Session Replay, $0.0001/request for Feature Flags) - see https://posthog.com/pricing and https://posthog.com/. profiles.name: Umami
profiles.why: Both companies lead their home pages with privacy compliance as the reason to switch off Google Analytics: Umami says it 'does not automatically collect personal information from your visitors, supporting GDPR and CCPA compliance out of the box' (umami.is/platform), while Plausible states it is 'built to enable you to comply with GDPR, CCPA and other privacy regulations' (E1). Where the two pages diverge is deployment and price: Umami's own pricing page frames self-hosting as free and open-source ('Umami is open-source and can be self-hosted for free'), whereas the cited Plausible pricing evidence shows its lowest published plan, Starter, at $9/month for one site with 3 years of retention (E328). This complicates rather than confirms the discovery hypothesis that self-hosting is chosen purely to avoid paying anyone: Umami itself also sells a usage-based Cloud plan starting at $0/month Hobby and $20/month Pro, so the free-self-host path and a paid-hosted path coexist inside the same company rather than cleanly separating 'free, self-hosted, technical buyer' from 'paid, hosted, non-technical buyer.'
profiles.discovery_reason: The self-hosted, open-source script a technical buyer or developer spins up themselves on their own server instead of paying anyone, especially before they've decided analytics is worth a subscription.
profiles.promise: Understand acquisition, behavior, conversion, and retention in one privacy-first platform. No cookies, no surveillance, set up in minutes.

Self-hosted open-source version is free to run on your own infrastructure.
